1. Core Clinical Tension: A 6-year-old girl residing in rural Lebanon with domestic sheep and dog contact presents with an indolent, slowly enlarging, painless left postauricular cystic neck mass in level V. CT imaging reveals a non-enhancing, unilocular fluid-filled lesion without soft tissue components. The clinical tension lies in distinguishing common benign congenital cervical cysts or lymphangiomas from an exceedingly rare primary hydatid cyst of the neck occurring outside the liver and lungs.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs after clinical presentation, physical examination, baseline blood work, neck ultrasonography, and contrast-enhanced CT define the cystic nature and anatomic boundaries of the level V mass, immediately prior to surgical excision, intraoperative visualization of the germinal membrane, and histopathology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Congenital branchial cleft anomalies (second branchial cleft cysts) are common in children but classically occur in the anterior triangle along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, whereas this cyst arose in the posterior triangle (level V) independent of the carotid sheath. Cystic hygroma / lymphangioma presents as a multilocular, infiltrative lesion crossing tissue planes, rather than a well-circumscribed unilocular cyst. Cold abscess (tuberculous lymphadenitis) typically displays peripheral rim enhancement, necrotic adenopathy, or systemic symptoms. The combination of pastoral canine/livestock exposure and a pristine unilocular fluid cyst raises suspicion for primary hydatid disease.
case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl presents to the otolaryngology clinic with a 3-month history of a slowly growing left postauricular cervical mass. Her family denies any history of fever, localized pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, or unintentional weight loss. The child resides in a rural area of Lebanon where livestock farming is common and sanitation infrastructure is limited; her family is of lower socioeconomic background and maintains close proximity to domesticated animals, including sheep and dogs.

On physical examination, the child is well-appearing and afebrile. Head and neck examination reveals an oval-shaped, soft, non-tender cervical mass in the left postauricular region. The overlying skin exhibits no erythema, warmth, or signs of inflammation. Palpation reveals no regional cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the physical examination is entirely unremarkable.

Routine laboratory testing is unremarkable, with normal complete blood count and inflammatory parameters. High-resolution neck ultrasonography demonstrates a well-circumscribed anechoic cystic mass measuring 34.7 × 28.6 mm in the left postauricular area without associated cervical adenopathy. Subsequent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck confirms a unilocular cystic mass located in level V, positioned posterior to the parotid gland and sternocleidomastoid muscle, anterior to the trapezius muscle, and independent of the carotid space. The mass is non-enhancing, sharply demarcated, and contains no internal septations, solid soft tissue components, or calcifications.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Congenital Cervical Cyst (Branchial Cleft Cyst / Cystic Hygroma)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: While an indolent, unilocular cystic cervical mass in a child frequently represents a congenital anomaly, branchial cleft cysts typically arise in the anterior triangle along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and cystic hygromas are typically multiseptated and infiltrative; this lesion was strictly unilocular and located in level V of the posterior triangle.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: It showed a level V unilocular cystic neck mass. It was seen posterior to the parotid gland and to sternocleidomastoid muscle, anterior to trapezius muscle, and independent from the carotid space. The mass was not enhancing, very well circumscribed, with no soft tissue component.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Malignant Cervical Neoplasm / Cystic Nodal Metastasis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Progressive cervical enlargement in a child warrants consideration of pediatric lymphoma or soft-tissue sarcoma; however, the complete absence of constitutional symptoms, normal laboratory workup, absence of adenopathy, and strictly cystic non-enhancing imaging appearance without solid components ruled out neoplasia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient's family denied any history of fever, pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, or weight loss... The mass looked benign, but it has been present for some time, slowly growing, and so the decision was taken to have it removed (Figure 1).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Complete surgical excision revealed a cyst containing clear fluid surrounded by a pearly white germinal membrane, with final histopathological examination confirming an echinococcal (hydatid) cyst occurring as a primary neck lesion in an endemic pastoral setting.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: During the procedure, the cyst partially ruptured, and it was found to contain clear fluid and surrounded by a white germinal membrane. Since the lesion did not raise oncologic concern, and given the characteristic features seen intraoperatively, which raised the suspicion for hydatid disease, a frozen section was not deemed necessary. The mass was sent for final pathology, which revealed an echinococcal cyst (hydatid cyst) (Figures 2 and 3).

editor_comments: Distilled strictly according to Stanford MedCaseReasoning CPC format. The case_prompt cleanly isolates outpatient ENT evaluation and CT imaging before surgical excision and pathology. Zero pathogen spoilers in prompt.
